title: Throttling Starlink Is a Disaster for Ukraine and the United States
text:
Throttling Starlink Is a Disaster for Ukraine and the United States

Photo: Dmytro Smolienko/ Ukrinform/Future Publishing/Getty Images

Commentary
by

Max Bergmann

Published October 22, 2026

The throttling of Starlink is a disaster not just for Ukraine, but potentially for the United States and global U.S. companies, especially in the defense and technology field. Whether or not it was an intentional act sanctioned by the U.S. government, the limitation of Ukrainian access to Starlink and its military companion, Starshield, is undermining Ukrainian drone operations on the front lines, contributing directly to the deaths of Ukrainian civilians, and setting ablaze U.S. credibility as a global provider of defense systems and technology. If not reversed, the consequences for the United States will be long lasting.Over the last several weeks, the relationship between Ukraine and the United States has collapsed. After the Trump administration struck a deal to waive sanctions on the sale of Russian diesel fuel, the White House pressed Ukraine to withhold further strikes on Russian energy infrastructure. Ukraine agreed to stop its strikes if Russia agreed in kind. Instead, Russia has escalated its air campaign against Ukrainian civilian infrastructure, targeting energy, ports, factories, data centers, and daily life in Kyiv. Ukraine’s subsequent counterattacks on Russian refineries have angered President Trump, leading him to attack President Zelensky on Truth Social. Soon after, Ukraine noticed that SpaceX’s Starlink and Starshield services were being disrupted, preventing its air-defense interceptor drones from being able to fly fast enough to shoot down Russia’s jet-powered drones, which have been terrorizing Ukrainian civilians. Starlink disruptions were also reportedly causing havoc on the front lines, impacting communications and drone operations, leading to fears that this could dramatically turn the tide in Russia’s favor. There was also a sudden lapse in intelligence sharing with Ukraine; the United States seemingly stopped sharing intelligence on incoming ballistic missile strikes (a charge the United States has denied). Ukrainians have an air raid alert app to alert them to incoming bombardment, giving them time to seek shelter. Instead, ballistic missiles exploded in Kyiv with no warning.However the facts unfold, the current global perception is that the United States has decided to punish Ukraine for continuing to strike Russia or for not ceding territory to Russia in the U.S. peace proposals. The problem for the Trump administration is that the United States now has fewer levers to pull and ultimately less leverage over Ukraine than it did when President Trump came into office in 2025. The current administration has stopped providing military and economic aid to Ukraine. Europe has taken over as the primary financier of Ukraine’s war effort and its economy, and increased European arms support have reduced its dependence on U.S. weapons and aid. Ukraine does not need the United States nearly as much as it did a year or two ago, but it does still depend on U.S. intelligence, satellite communications technology, and high-end ballistic missile defense Patriot systems. This is the last remaining area where the United States wields real leverage over Ukraine. The problem with the Trump administration pulling this lever, however, is that it is functionally the “nuclear” option—mutually assured destruction with devastating long-term consequences for the United States. Leaving Ukraine defenseless would cause profound damage to America’s image; the transatlantic alliance and U.S. global business could face significant, if not generational, consequences.This is because satellite services in Ukraine have already been paid for. Ukraine’s contract with Starshield is being paid for through a normal Foreign Military Sale with the U.S. government, and Starlink through a commercial contract (paid for by Poland). In this sense, if the United States were intentionally slowing down Starlink, it would not be holding back aid; it would be withholding a service. This would be perceived as the United States defaulting on contractual obligations, and, in so doing, make the United States an unreliable supplier of military and commercial defense and technology systems. While U.S. intelligence sharing, including targeting information and advance air warning, is not paid for, the United States still derives tremendous benefits. Working intimately with the Ukrainians allows U.S. European Command and U.S. companies to gain a keen understanding of the evolving nature of modern warfare and assess the performance of U.S. military systems under fire. This is, in fact, a mutually beneficial arrangement—but ultimately, the United States does it because it saves lives.Trust in the United States as a security provider has been built up over nearly a century among global allies and partners, and this trust has proved crucial to the success of U.S. businesses. For Europeans who relied on U.S. military protection, it made sense to also buy U.S. weapons. And if Europe was buying U.S. weapons, why not also buy U.S. technology? U.S. companies gained tremendous market share in Europe especially, with Europeans buying roughly 60 percent of their weapons imports from the United States and Europe is responsible for a significant share of the global profits for U.S. tech companies.. But now Europeans, and U.S. allies and partners around the world, are seeing the United States pull the rug out from under Ukraine, resulting in death and destruction to the benefit of Russia. If allies cannot trust the United States to defend them, how can they trust doing business with the United States?Perhaps it is not too late to pull back from the brink. The Trump administration has denied restricting or cutting off access to these services, pointing instead to Elon Musk. There is time to restore them as they were. But if they remain heavily curtailed, the damage will be incalculable. It will prompt allies in Europe and across the world to aggressively work to reduce their reliance on the United States. Instead of de-risking from China, Europe and other allies will de-risk from the United States, working with haste to develop alternative systems and to reduce exposure to U.S. technology and defense systems. These systems will likely be less capable and more costly. But they will be theirs. European and global competitors will emerge, and U.S. company profits will suffer as they are increasingly passed over. Indeed, this is already happening. The implications for NATO are also dire. Failure to restore these vital services to Ukraine would amount to the United States taking a giant step to remove itself from the NATO alliance. Europeans would have to assume they simply cannot rely on the United States and doubt whether the United States would come to their defense if Russian drones were attacking them. An alliance built on trust cannot survive if desperation is seen as an opportunity to extract concessions.Trust in the United States, built over decades, it turns out, can be destroyed in as little time as it takes a Russian jet-powered drone to strike a playground in Kyiv. Undermining Ukraine’s ability to defend itself would be an epic mistake.Max Bergmann is the director of the Europe, Russia, and Eurasia Program and the Stuart Center in Euro-Atlantic and Northern European Studies at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).
